image_description: A close-up, high-angle shot of a sea lion resting on a rocky surface. The animal is lying on its side with its head tucked down, eyes closed. One large foreflipper is prominently visible in the foreground, draped over a rock. The fur appears short, coarse, and brownish-tan, transitioning to darker shades on the head. The background consists of out-of-focus grey rocks.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is visible but the angle (side profile, resting) and potential female sex make the sagittal crest indistinguishable or absent. It does not clearly match the 'prominent' description.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: A small, distinct external ear flap is visible on the side of the head, confirming it is a sea lion and not a true seal.
Dark, stiff whiskers are clearly visible protruding from the snout area.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The texture appears consistent with short, coarse fur. The color is brownish-tan on the back/side. Ventral surface is mostly occluded but the visible transition seems consistent.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the body shows a smooth, tapered shape typical of pinnipeds.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: There is no visible thick neck mane; the neck area blends smoothly into the shoulders. This suggests the subject is likely a female or juvenile, so the male-specific trait is absent.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreground flipper is large and broad. While the 'hairless underside' isn't fully exposed due to the angle, the structure matches the description of a sea lion foreflipper.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The hind flippers are completely occluded by the body and the rocks in this framing.
Due to the resting pose and camera angle, only one side of the body is clearly visible, making symmetry verification impossible.

artifact_observations.location: Flipper edges and rock contact points
artifact_observations.reasoning: Slight softness/blurring at the boundary between the flipper and the rock, lacking the sharp micro-contrast expected in a high-resolution macro shot. Possible minor edge bleeding.

The transition from head to body is very smooth, almost melting into the background rocks slightly. It lacks distinct anatomical definition of the shoulder girdle, though this could be due to the resting pose.
